Abstract.AbstractText: Vibrio parahaemolyticus (Vp) and Vibrio vulnificus (Vv) are naturally occurring estuarine bacteria and are the leading causes of seafood-associated infections and mortality in the USA. Though multiple-antibiotic resistant Vp and Vv have been reported resistance patterns in vibrios are not as well documented as other food-borne bacterial pathogens. Salinity relaying (SR) is a Post-Harvest Processing (PHP) treatment to reduce the abundance of these pathogens in shellfish harvested during the warmer months. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the antimicrobial susceptibility (AMS), pathogenicity and genetic profiles of Vp and Vv recovered from oysters during an oyster relay study. Isolates [Vp (n=296) and Vv (n=94)] were recovered from oysters before and during the 21day relaying study to detect virulence genes (tdh and trh) and genes correlated with virulence (vcgC) using multiplex q-PCR. AMS to 20 different antibiotics was investigated using micro broth dilution, and Pulsed-Field Gel Electrophoresis (PFGE) was used to study the genetic profiles of isolates. Twenty percent of Vv isolates were vcgC+, while 1 and 2% of Vp were tdh+ and trh+, respectively. More than 77% of Vv and 30% of Vp isolates were resistant to at least one antimicrobial. Forty-eight percent of Vv and 8% of Vp isolates were resistant to two or more antimicrobials. All isolates demonstrated a high genetic diversity, even among those isolated from the same site and having a similar AMS profile. No significant effect of the relaying process on AMS, virulence genes, or PFGE profiles of Vv and Vp was observed.IMPORTANCE Analysis of the antibiotic resistance profiles of Vv and Vp isolated from oysters during this study indicated that more than 48% of Vv isolates were resistant to two or more antimicrobials including those recommended by CDC for treating Vibrio infections. Also the Vp isolates showed high Minimum Inhibitory Concentrations for some of the Vibrio infection treatment antibiotics. Monitoring of AMS profiles of this bacterium is important to ensure optimal treatment of infections and improve food safety. Our study showed no significant differences in AMS profiles of Vv (p=0.26) and Vp (p=0.23) isolated from the oysters collected before versus after relaying. This suggests that the salinity of the relaying sites did not affect AMS profile of the Vibrio isolates, although it did reduce the number of these bacteria in oysters (S. Parveen, M. Jahncke, S. Elmahdi, H. Crocker, J. Bowers, C. White, S. Gray, and K. Brohawn. J Food Sci. 82 (2):484-491, 2017).
